extracted.intended_audience: students, scholars, and practitioners of natural philosophy/science interested in Baconian method and the philosophy of scientific inquiry
extracted.subtask_description: Aphoristic guidance (Francis Bacon) on interpreting nature: aims of inquiry, the primacy of discovering 'forms', two kinds of transformative axioms, and practical rules for experimental method and investigation of latent processes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish aims: generation/superinduction vs discovery of form
rubrics_metrics.description: To generate and superinduce a new nature upon a given body is the labor of human power; to discover the form or true difference of a given nature is the labor and discovery of human knowledge. Two subordinate labors are (a) transformation of concrete bodies from one to another and (b) discovery, in every species of generation and motion, of the latent and uninterrupted process from manifest efficient and subject-matter up to the given form (and likewise the latent conformation of bodies at rest).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This distinguishes practical art (making new natures) from theoretical science (discovering forms), and sets out secondary but related tasks. It frames what a method for natural inquiry must aim at: either productive transformation or explanatory discovery of latent processes and conformations.

rubrics_metrics.name: True knowledge is deduced from causes (four causes)
rubrics_metrics.description: True knowledge is that which is deduced from causes. The four causes (matter, form, efficient, and end/final cause) are a useful division, though the final cause often corrupts the sciences except in human affairs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasizes cause-based explanations rather than mere appearances or rhetoric. Warns that appeal to final causes (teleology) generally misleads scientific inquiry and that investigators should focus on discovering operative causes, especially 'form'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primacy of discovering 'form' over mere efficient/material causes
rubrics_metrics.description: Discovery of the form is more valuable: knowing efficient and material causes alone gives limited and superficial knowledge; knowledge of the form reveals unity across diverse substances and yields genuine theory and broad practical power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If one learns only particular efficient/material causes, one obtains only partial, context-limited power; discovering a form (that which inherently produces a nature) enables invention of things otherwise unattainable by experiment or chance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characteristics of a proper practical method: certain, free, and preparatory
rubrics_metrics.description: A genuine and perfect rule of practice should be (1) certain (neither fail in effect nor deceive in trial), (2) free (not restrict the practitioner to peculiar means unavailable to others), and (3) preparatory (approachable and not more difficult than the desired effect).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When giving precepts for producing a nature (e.g., superinducing yellowness of gold on silver), the method must reliably work, allow alternative means, and be attainable in practice. These three conditions together coincide with discovering the true form.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of a true form (necessary-and-sufficient marker)
rubrics_metrics.description: The true form of any nature is such that it is always present when that nature is present and absent when that nature is absent; its removal makes the nature vanish. It deduces the particular nature from some source of essence existing in many subjects (a real genus).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A correct theoretical axiom/form must be both necessary and sufficient for the nature: it must universally attest presence/absence and explain the origin of the nature by reference to a more general, known substrate. This logical-convertibility criterion guides identification of forms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Axiom type 1 — transform by composing aggregate simple natures (primary)
rubrics_metrics.description: One kind of axiom regards the body as an aggregate of simple natures: by acquiring forms and methods for producing simple natures (e.g., yellowness, weight, ductility), and their degrees and modes, one can consider how to unite them to transform a body (primary action).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This primary method builds transformations from constant, eternal, and universal simple natures (example: enumerate and reproduce gold's simple properties to 'make' gold). It underlies the highest, radical operations of human power and starts from universal constants in nature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Axiom type 2 — transform by discovering latent processes in concrete bodies (secondary)
rubrics_metrics.description: The second kind of axiom proceeds by investigating concrete bodies as they occur in nature and tracing the latent and uninterrupted processes by which they are generated (e.g., generation of metals, plants, animals) rather than by composing simple natures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This approach—reconstructing the natural sequence from beginnings to finished product—often appears more prompt, practical, and promising for operative work, but it is distinct from and subordinate to primary axioms based on simple natures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Operative branch vs contemplative branch; dependence on primary axioms
rubrics_metrics.description: The operative (practical) branch extends from observed nature to nearby subjects and immediate applications; higher and radical operations upon nature depend entirely on the primary axioms concerning simple natures. Even fields where action is impossible (e.g., astronomy) must refer their investigations to primary universal axioms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical manipulation often uses latent-process axioms for immediate results, but ultimate control and broad theoretical understanding require primary axioms. The investigator should seek primary laws (e.g., spontaneous rotation, attraction) to ground conclusions even in observational sciences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Investigate latent processes by exhaustive causal sequencing and attention to small efforts
rubrics_metrics.description: To discover latent processes we must inquire what is lost, what remains, what is added, what is diluted, contracted, united, separated, continuous or broken off, what urges forward or impedes, what predominates or is subservient, etc. Natural acts are often brought about by the smallest efforts, too small for ordinary senses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A methodical, detailed analysis of each stage, increment and minor agent in a process is required—including scrutiny of minute, otherwise imperceptible forces—because these small efforts frequently govern transformations and motions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical usefulness and theoretical correctness coincide
rubrics_metrics.description: The practical and theoretical rules are in fact the same: that which is most useful in practice is most correct in theory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bacon asserts that a precept useful for producing effects (practical) will tend to be the correct theoretical description of the underlying form; thus practical success is a key test of theoretical validity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer demonstrations appropriate to the subject; distrust evidence that merely flatters inclinations
rubrics_metrics.description: One should suspect that kind of evidence most consonant to our inclinations and not admit any notion as real except when it can be based firmly upon the demonstration peculiar to the subject (not merely upon our impressions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid allowing personal preferences, aesthetic tastes, or favored methods (e.g., applying number or geometry where inappropriate) to bias acceptance of claims; let the method of proof fit the nature of the inquiry. Examples: Pythagorean numerology or geometric reasoning about the soul are admissible only when suited to the subject.
